analysis.one_liner: Strips patent monopolies from drugmakers who charge Americans more than other countries pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and referred to two House committees, where it has sat with no action, no hearings, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make the Department of Health and Human Services review all brand-name drug prices every year against median prices in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan. If a drug costs more here than the median price abroad, the government would strip the manufacturer's exclusive rights, license any company to make a generic version, and require the licensed copies to be sold below the excessive price. It would also create a public database of price determinations and require drugmakers to disclose what they spend on research and advertising. It has not received any action beyond its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs, especially expensive ones, plus taxpayers and insurers who pay those prices. If a drug is found excessively priced, generic and biosimilar makers could enter the market with an expedited 8-month review and would have to sell below the excessive price [S3].

how_it_helps.text: HHS would review every brand-name drug's price at least annually, using median prices in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan as the benchmark, with a public database showing which drugs were found excessive.

For a drug found excessively priced, the government would void its exclusivities and issue open, non-exclusive licenses letting any company make a cheaper generic or biosimilar, with expedited 8-month review of those applications.
Anyone could petition HHS for a determination on a drug, and the bill bars manufacturers from anticompetitive behavior that interferes with the licenses.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose exclusive rights and pricing power the bill would take away when they charge US prices above foreign medians, and who would face detailed annual financial reporting with penalties of up to 1% of a drug's daily gross revenue for noncompliance [S3].

drawbacks.text: It would strip exclusive patent rights from manufacturers whose US prices exceed median prices in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan — a company could lose monopoly control over a drug it invented and tested, which brand-name manufacturers argue undercuts the profits that pay for developing new drugs.

Generic or biosimilar versions sold under an open license would still pay a reasonable royalty and could take months to enter the market, so price relief for any given drug would not be immediate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large — prescription drug prices in the US run well above the prices other wealthy countries pay, and opening the market to generics when prices are out of line directly lowers costs for patients, insurers, and taxpayers. The main costs and risks: generic entry can take time even after licenses are issued, and weaker effective exclusivity could somewhat reduce the profits that fund pharmaceutical research, particularly for marginal drugs. The bill preserves reasonable royalties and development-cost review, which softens but does not eliminate that concern. On balance, the public benefit of ending above-world-price monopolies outweighs the research-incentive cost, though the bill's design depends heavily on how aggressively HHS administers it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 21, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees the same day.
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral.
It drew only 4 cosponsors, all House Democrats, out of 217.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers keep their exclusive rights and their freedom to set US prices above what other countries pay. Patients and insurers keep paying those prices.

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its preceding versions of the same proposal.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and have taken no action on it since May 2025.

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.what_they_did: The bill was never scheduled for floor consideration; the referral structure gave the Republican-controlled committees and leadership full discretion over whether it would advance.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has consistently opposed measures that would undercut patent exclusivity or reference international drug prices.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and with Republicans controlling the House and its committees the bill has received no consideration.

industries.note: The bill would void their government-granted exclusivities and open their patents to any competitor whenever US prices exceed median prices in five peer countries, and require detailed financial reporting on pricing, research, and marketing. It directly attacks the pricing power that makes US drugs the most expensive in the world.
They would gain the right to make and sell licensed versions of excessively priced brand-name drugs with expedited FDA review, creating a large new market for them and cheaper options for patients.

analysis.trajectory: With only 4 cosponsors, no hearings or markup in either committee of referral, and a Republican House majority that has not taken it up, the bill will very likely die quietly at the end of the Congress without a vote, as previous versions of this proposal have.
